units.text: A foundation LLM, also called a base LLM or a pre-trained LLM, is a general-purpose large language model.
A foundation LLM is trained on enough natural language to learn a great deal about grammar, words and idioms.
A foundation LLM can generate helpful sentences about the topics it was trained on and can perform creative tasks such as writing poetry.
However, a foundation LLM is not a complete solution for machine learning tasks such as classification or regression.
For classification and regression tasks, a foundation LLM serves as a platform rather than a complete solution.
Fine-tuning turns a foundation LLM into a solution for a specific application.
Distillation is a secondary process that creates a smaller version of a fine-tuned LLM with fewer parameters.

units.text: Foundation LLMs recognize patterns so well that foundation LLMs often need only a modest amount of additional training to perform a specific task.
This additional training is called fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning trains a foundation LLM on examples that are specific to the task of the application.
Engineers can often fine-tune a foundation LLM with only a few hundred to a few thousand training examples.
Standard fine-tuning is computationally expensive, because standard fine-tuning updates the weights and biases of every parameter on each backpropagation iteration.
Parameter-efficient tuning is a less expensive alternative to standard fine-tuning, because parameter-efficient tuning updates only a subset of the parameters on each backpropagation iteration.
A fine-tuned LLM usually makes better predictions on its task than the foundation LLM does.
A fine-tuned LLM has the same number of parameters as the foundation LLM it came from.
For example, fine-tuning a foundation LLM that has ten billion parameters produces a fine-tuned LLM that also has ten billion parameters.

A teacher model can also give the student model a numerical score instead of a binary label.
A numerical score gives the student model a richer training signal than a binary label does.
The richer training signal helps the student model predict borderline cases as well as clearly positive cases and clearly negative cases.

relation_proposals.evidence_context: Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM.

relation_proposals.evidence_context: Online inference generates predictions at the time a request is served. Some LLMs are too large for online inference to be practical for tasks such as regression or classification. For this reason, many engineering teams use offline inference instead of online inference. Offline inference, also called bulk inference or static inference, means that an LLM generates predictions in advance and caches the predictions, rather than generating predictions at serving time. Offline inference saves computing resources and makes it possible to use larger LLMs. Slow prediction is acceptable for a task that runs only weekly or monthly. For example, Google Search used an LLM in offline inference to cache a list of more than 800 synonyms for Covid vaccines in more than 50 languages. Google Search then used the cached list to identify queries about vaccines in live traffic. LLMs generally inherit biases from the data used to train the LLM and from the data used to distill the LLM. For this reason, LLMs should be used fairly and responsibly.

units.text: Online inference generates predictions at the time a request is served.
Some LLMs are too large for online inference to be practical for tasks such as regression or classification.
For this reason, many engineering teams use offline inference instead of online inference.
Offline inference, also called bulk inference or static inference, means that an LLM generates predictions in advance and caches the predictions, rather than generating predictions at serving time.
Offline inference saves computing resources and makes it possible to use larger LLMs.
Slow prediction is acceptable for a task that runs only weekly or monthly.
For example, Google Search used an LLM in offline inference to cache a list of more than 800 synonyms for Covid vaccines in more than 50 languages.
Google Search then used the cached list to identify queries about vaccines in live traffic.
LLMs generally inherit biases from the data used to train the LLM and from the data used to distill the LLM.
For this reason, LLMs should be used fairly and responsibly.

outline.overview: This chapter defines foundation LLMs as general-purpose models with limitations for specific tasks, explaining how fine-tuning adapts them to applications while distillation optimizes them into smaller, faster versions. It contrasts standard parameter updates with efficient tuning methods and addresses the resource costs of large models versus the accuracy trade-offs in distilled ones. The text details bulk inference distillation where teacher models generate rich numerical labels for student models, alongside prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot) that customize outputs without altering parameters. Finally, it compares online and offline inference strategies, citing Google Search's cached predictions for low-frequency tasks while emphasizing ethical considerations regarding model biases.
topics: Foundation LLM definition and general capabilities
Limitations of foundation models for specific ML tasks
Fine-tuning mechanisms: standard vs. parameter-efficient approaches
Training data requirements and computational costs
Distillation process: creating smaller, faster models
Trade-off between model size/parameters and prediction accuracy
Bulk inference distillation: teacher-student dynamics
Richness of numerical vs. binary labeling signals
Prompt engineering: zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot techniques
Online vs. offline inference methods
Resource efficiency in static/bulk inference deployments
Ethical usage and inherent model biases

segments.summary: The text defines a foundation LLM as a general-purpose model trained on natural language to understand grammar and perform creative tasks, noting its limitations for specific machine learning tasks like classification or regression where it serves only as a platform. It explains that fine-tuning converts the foundation model into a specific application solution, while distillation creates smaller versions of these fine-tuned models.
topics: Definition and capabilities of foundation LLMs
Limitations of foundation LLMs for specific tasks
Role of fine-tuning in creating application-specific solutions
Function of distillation in model optimization

segments.summary: Foundation LLMs require modest additional training called fine-tuning to perform specific tasks using few hundred to thousand examples. While standard fine-tuning updates all parameters and is computationally expensive, parameter-efficient tuning offers a cheaper alternative by updating only a subset of parameters. Both methods result in a fine-tuned model with the same number of parameters as the foundation model but improved task-specific predictions.
topics: Foundation LLM pattern recognition capabilities
Definition and purpose of fine-tuning
Training data requirements for fine-tuning
Computational cost of standard fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient tuning
Parameter update mechanisms in backpropagation
Performance improvement of fine-tuned models
Conservation of parameter count during fine-tuning

segments.summary: Fine-tuned LLMs possess large parameter counts, necessitating significant computational and environmental resources for prediction generation, often including irrelevant parameters. Distillation addresses this by creating smaller models that generate predictions faster and with fewer resources, though these distilled models typically yield somewhat worse predictions compared to their larger counterparts, as models with more parameters generally outperform those with fewer.
topics: High parameter count in fine-tuned LLMs
Computational and environmental resource demands
Irrelevance of many parameters to specific applications
Distillation process for creating smaller LLMs
Efficiency gains: faster generation and reduced resources in distilled models
Accuracy trade-off: worse predictions in distilled models
General rule: more parameters lead to better predictions

segments.summary: The chapter segment describes bulk inference distillation where a larger teacher LLM labels data to train a smaller student LLM, enabling knowledge transfer for tasks like real-time comment moderation. It highlights that teachers can generate more labeled data than their own training set and provide numerical scores instead of binary labels, offering richer signals that improve prediction accuracy on borderline cases.
topics: Bulk inference distillation mechanism
Teacher-student model roles
Real-time application example (toxicity scoring)
Data generation capacity of teacher models
Numerical vs. binary labeling signals

segments.summary: Prompt engineering enables end users to customize LLM outputs by providing context through examples or instructions without altering model parameters. Techniques include one-shot prompting (one example), few-shot prompting (multiple examples acting as training data), and zero-shot prompting (no examples, which may yield ambiguous results like confusing the fruit 'apple' with the technology company).
topics: Definition of prompt engineering as customization via user input rather than parameter changes
One-shot prompting: supplying a single example to guide response patterns
Few-shot prompting: using multiple examples that function as training data for context
Zero-shot prompting: operating without examples and its susceptibility to ambiguity
Mechanism of prompt engineering relying on existing pattern-recognition abilities

segments.summary: The segment contrasts online and offline inference methods for Large Language Models (LLMs), highlighting that offline inference involves pre-generating and caching predictions to save resources and enable the use of larger models, particularly for low-frequency tasks. It cites Google Search's use of cached LLM predictions for vaccine synonym identification as an example, while also noting the necessity of fair and responsible usage due to inherent model biases.

The teacher model labels a dataset, and the labeled dataset is used to train the student model. Through the labels, the teacher model passes its knowledge to the student model. reviews.evidence_context: Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM.

reviews.evidence_context: Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM.

facts.evidence_context: The most common form of distillation uses bulk inference to label data. In this form of distillation, the larger LLM acts as a teacher model and the smaller LLM acts as a student model. The teacher model labels a dataset, and the labeled dataset is used to train the student model. Through the labels, the teacher model passes its knowledge to the student model. For example, to moderate comments in real time, a team could run a large toxicity-scoring model offline to label training data, and then use the labeled data to distill a student model small enough to score live comments. A teacher model can sometimes produce more labeled data than the teacher model itself was trained on. A teacher model can also give the student model a numerical score instead of a binary label. A numerical score gives the student model a richer training signal than a binary label does. The richer training signal helps the student model predict borderline cases as well as clearly positive cases and clearly negative cases.

facts.evidence_context: Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM.

facts.evidence_context: Online inference generates predictions at the time a request is served. Some LLMs are too large for online inference to be practical for tasks such as regression or classification. For this reason, many engineering teams use offline inference instead of online inference. Offline inference, also called bulk inference or static inference, means that an LLM generates predictions in advance and caches the predictions, rather than generating predictions at serving time. Offline inference saves computing resources and makes it possible to use larger LLMs. Slow prediction is acceptable for a task that runs only weekly or monthly. For example, Google Search used an LLM in offline inference to cache a list of more than 800 synonyms for Covid vaccines in more than 50 languages. Google Search then used the cached list to identify queries about vaccines in live traffic. LLMs generally inherit biases from the data used to train the LLM and from the data used to distill the LLM. For this reason, LLMs should be used fairly and responsibly.

  {
    "id": "paragraph_001",
    "order": 0,
    "start": 0,
    "end": 772,
    "text": "A foundation LLM, also called a base LLM or a pre-trained LLM, is a general-purpose large language model. A foundation LLM is trained on enough natural language to learn a great deal about grammar, words and idioms. A foundation LLM can generate helpful sentences about the topics it was trained on and can perform creative tasks such as writing poetry. However, a foundation LLM is not a complete solution for machine learning tasks such as classification or regression. For classification and regression tasks, a foundation LLM serves as a platform rather than a complete solution. Fine-tuning turns a foundation LLM into a solution for a specific application. Distillation is a secondary process that creates a smaller version of a fine-tuned LLM with fewer parameters."
  },
  {
    "id": "paragraph_002",
    "order": 1,
    "start": 774,
    "end": 1850,
    "text": "Foundation LLMs recognize patterns so well that foundation LLMs often need only a modest amount of additional training to perform a specific task. This additional training is called fine-tuning. Fine-tuning trains a foundation LLM on examples that are specific to the task of the application. Engineers can often fine-tune a foundation LLM with only a few hundred to a few thousand training examples. Standard fine-tuning is computationally expensive, because standard fine-tuning updates the weights and biases of every parameter on each backpropagation iteration. Parameter-efficient tuning is a less expensive alternative to standard fine-tuning, because parameter-efficient tuning updates only a subset of the parameters on each backpropagation iteration. A fine-tuned LLM usually makes better predictions on its task than the foundation LLM does. A fine-tuned LLM has the same number of parameters as the foundation LLM it came from. For example, fine-tuning a foundation LLM that has ten billion parameters produces a fine-tuned LLM that also has ten billion parameters."
  },
  {
    "id": "paragraph_003",
    "order": 2,
    "start": 1852,
    "end": 2503,
    "text": "Fine-tuned LLMs usually have a very large number of parameters. As a result, generating predictions with a fine-tuned LLM requires large computational and environmental resources. Many of those parameters are typically irrelevant to a specific application. Distillation creates a smaller LLM from a larger LLM. The distilled LLM generates predictions faster and requires fewer computational and environmental resources than the larger LLM. However, the predictions of the distilled LLM are generally somewhat worse than the predictions of the larger LLM. LLMs with more parameters almost always make better predictions than LLMs with fewer parameters."
  },
  {
    "id": "paragraph_004",
    "order": 3,
    "start": 2505,
    "end": 3515,
    "text": "The most common form of distillation uses bulk inference to label data. In this form of distillation, the larger LLM acts as a teacher model and the smaller LLM acts as a student model. The teacher model labels a dataset, and the labeled dataset is used to train the student model. Through the labels, the teacher model passes its knowledge to the student model. For example, to moderate comments in real time, a team could run a large toxicity-scoring model offline to label training data, and then use the labeled data to distill a student model small enough to score live comments. A teacher model can sometimes produce more labeled data than the teacher model itself was trained on. A teacher model can also give the student model a numerical score instead of a binary label. A numerical score gives the student model a richer training signal than a binary label does. The richer training signal helps the student model predict borderline cases as well as clearly positive cases and clearly negative cases."
  },
  {
    "id": "paragraph_005",
    "order": 4,
    "start": 3517,
    "end": 4644,
    "text": "Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM."
  },
  {
    "id": "paragraph_006",
    "order": 5,
    "start": 4646,
    "end": 5686,
    "text": "Online inference generates predictions at the time a request is served. Some LLMs are too large for online inference to be practical for tasks such as regression or classification. For this reason, many engineering teams use offline inference instead of online inference. Offline inference, also called bulk inference or static inference, means that an LLM generates predictions in advance and caches the predictions, rather than generating predictions at serving time. Offline inference saves computing resources and makes it possible to use larger LLMs. Slow prediction is acceptable for a task that runs only weekly or monthly. For example, Google Search used an LLM in offline inference to cache a list of more than 800 synonyms for Covid vaccines in more than 50 languages. Google Search then used the cached list to identify queries about vaccines in live traffic. LLMs generally inherit biases from the data used to train the LLM and from the data used to distill the LLM. For this reason, LLMs should be used fairly and responsibly."
  }

Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit.
